nobility.e: From Old French nobilité, from Latin nobilitas. Equivalent to noble + -ity.
nobility.g: A noble or privileged social class, historically accompanied by a hereditary title; aristocracy.

noble.e: From Middle English noble, from Old French noble, borrowed from Latin nōbilis (“knowable, known, well-known, famous, celebrated, high-born, of noble birth, excellent”), from nōscere, gnōscere (“to know”). False cognate of Arabic نبيل (nabīl).
noble.g: An aristocrat; one of aristocratic blood.

nobody.e: From Middle English nobody, no-body, no body. By surface analysis, no (“none, not any”, adjective) + body (“one, person, individual”).
nobody.g: Not any person; the logical negation of somebody.

nocturnal.e: From Middle French nocturnal, from Late Latin nocturnālis (“nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”), from Latin nox (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”).
nocturnal.g: Of a person, creature, group, or species, primarily active during the night.

noise.e: From Middle English noyse, noise, from Old French noise (“a dispute, wrangle, strife, noise”), of uncertain origin. According to some, from Latin nausia, nausea (“disgust, nausea”); according to others, from Latin noxia (“hurt, harm, damage, injury”); but neither explanation is satisfactory in regard to either form or sense.
noise.g: Various sounds, usually unwanted or unpleasant.

noisome.e: From Middle English noysom; equivalent to noy + -some (short for annoy, from an(n)oien, enoien from Anglo-Norman anuier, from Old French enuier (French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiare, from in- (intensive prefix) + odium (“hate”)).

nomad.e: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming, wandering, esp. to find pasture”), from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “pasture”).
nomad.g: A member of a society or class who herd animals from pasture to pasture with no fixed home.

none.e: From Middle English none, noon, non (“not one”), from Old English nān (“not one, not any, none”), from Proto-West Germanic *nain, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz (“none, nought, nothing”), equivalent to ne (“not”) + one.
none.g: Not any of a given number or group.

none.e: From French none, from Latin nōna (“ninth; ninth hour”).
none.g: Alternative form of nones: the ninth hour after dawn; (Christianity) the religious service appointed to this hour.

nonsense.e: From non- (“no, none, lack of”) + sense, from c. 1610.
nonsense.g: Letters or words, in writing or speech, that have no meaning or pattern or seem to have no meaning.

noon.e: From Middle English noen, none, non, from Old English nōn (“the ninth hour”), from a Germanic borrowing of classical Latin nōna (“ninth hour”) (short for nōna hōra), feminine of nōnus (“ninth”).
noon.g: The time of day when the Sun seems to reach its highest point in the sky; solar noon.

noonday.g: The time of noon; the time of day when the sun is highest in the sky, especially on a hot day.

noontide.e: From Middle English non-tyde, from Old English nōntīd (“noontide”), equivalent to noon + tide.

noose.e: From Middle English nose (“noose, loop”), of unclear origin. Possibly from Old French nos or Old Occitan nous, nos, nominative singular or accusative plural of nou (“knot”), with a required change in meaning shifting from the "knot" itself to the "loop" created by the knot.
noose.g: An adjustable loop of rope, such as the one placed around the neck in hangings, or the one at the end of a lasso.

normal.e: From Latin normālis (“made according to a carpenter's square; later: according to a rule”), from nōrma (“carpenter's square”), of uncertain origin; equivalent to norm + -al, doublet of normale. The earliest meaning of the word in English was "perpendicular.
normal.g: According to norms or rules or to a regular pattern.

north.e: From Middle English north, from Old English norþ, from Proto-West Germanic *norþr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nér (“below (the surface)”). The meaning developed either from "region where the sun is below (the earth)" or from "left side of someone who turns to the east when praying".
north.g: The direction towards the pole to the left-hand side of someone facing east, specifically 0°, or (on another celestial object) the direction

northern.e: From Middle English northerne, from Old English norþerne, from Proto-West Germanic *norþrōnī, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz. Morphologically north + -ern.
northern.g: Of, facing, situated in, or related to the north; northerly.

northwest.e: From Middle English northwest, from Old English norþwest, equivalent to north + west.
northwest.g: The intercardinal compass point halfway between west and north; specifically at a bearing of 315°.

nose.e: From Middle English nose, from Old English nosu, from Proto-West Germanic *nosu, variant of *nasō, old dual from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s- ~ *nh₂es- (“nose, nostril”).
nose.g: A protuberance on the face housing the nostrils, which are used to breathe or smell.

nostril.e: From Middle English nostrille, from Old English nosþyrel. By surface analysis, nose + thirl (“hole”).
nostril.g: Either of the two orifices located on the nose (or on the beak of a bird); used as a passage for air and other gases to travel the nasal pas

notable.e: From Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy, extraordinary”), from notō (“to note, mark”); in some senses from Middle English note (“benefit, profit, use, advantage”), from Old English notu (“t-use, profit, advantage, employment”) + -able.
notable.g: Worthy of note; remarkable; memorable; noted or distinguished.

note.e: From Middle English note, from Old English not, nōt (“note, mark, sign”) and Old French note (“letter, note”), both from Latin nota (“mark, sign, remark, note”).

From Middle English note (“use, usefulness, profit”), from Old English notu (“use, enjoyment, advantage, profit, utility”), from Proto-West Germanic *notu, from Proto-Germanic *nutō (“enjoyment, utilisation”), from Proto-Indo-European *newd- (“to acquire, make use of”).
note.g: That which is needed or necessary; business; duty; work.

nothing.e: From Middle English nothyng, noon thing, non thing, na þing, nan thing, nan þing, from Old English nāþing, nān þing (“nothing”, literally “not any thing”), equivalent to no + thing.

notice.e: Borrowed from Middle French notice, from the Latin nōtitia.

notion.e: From Latin nōtiō (“a becoming acquainted, a taking cognizance, an examination, an investigation, a conception, idea, notion”), from nōscō (“to know”).
notion.g: Mental apprehension of whatever may be known, thought, or imagined; idea, concept.

notorious.e: From Late Middle English notoryous, from Medieval Latin nōtōrius (“evident, known; famous, well-known; infamous”), from Latin nōtus (“known, recognized; familiar, widely known; famous, well-known; infamous”) + -tōrius (suffix forming adjectives). Nōtus is the perfect passive participle of nōscō (“to become acquainted with or learn about (something).

notwithstanding.e: From Middle English notwithstandinge, notwithstondyng, natwithstandyng, equivalent to not + withstanding.

nought.e: From Middle English nought, noght, noȝt, from Old English nōwiht, nāwiht, which in turn comes from ne-ā-wiht, which was a phrase used as an emphatic "no", meaning "not anything". Equivalent to ne + ought or ne + a + wight.
nought.g: A thing or person of no worth or value; nil.

nourish.e: From Middle English norischen, from Old French nouriss-, stem of one of the conjugated forms of norrir, from Latin nutriō (“to suckle, feed, foster, nourish, cherish, preserve, support”).

nourisher.g: One who, or that which, nourishes.

nourishment.e: From Middle English norisshement, from Middle French, from Old French norissement, from norrir, equivalent to nourish + -ment.
nourishment.g: The act of nourishing or the state of being nourished.

novice.e: From Middle English novice, novys, from Anglo-Norman novice, Middle French novice, itself borrowed from Latin novīcius, later novitius (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late Latin as a noun, masculine novicius, feminine novicia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”)), from novus (“new”).
novice.g: A beginner; one who is not very familiar or experienced in a particular subject.

now.e: From Middle English nou, nu, from Old English nū, from Proto-West Germanic *nū, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”).

nowhere.e: From Middle English nowher, from Old English nōhwēr, nāhwǣr, from nā- + hwǣr. By surface analysis, no + where. Adjective usage is taken from phrases like nowhere on the map (signifying the location was too small or too insignificant to be listed), nowhere you want to be, etc.
